name: Ptosis-correcting Korean eye-opening surgery

lead:
This procedure pairs ptosis correction, which raises the upper eyelid by tightening or reattaching the lid-lifting muscle, with double-eyelid (East Asian blepharoplasty) surgery, which forms a crease. Together they expose more of the eye.
Patients seek it for larger, more alert-looking eyes; it is popular in South Korea and other East Asian countries, where double-eyelid surgery is among the most common aesthetic procedures.

paras: An ophthalmic plastic or cosmetic surgeon assesses lid height and muscle function, then performs levator advancement or a sling technique along with crease formation, sometimes with epicanthoplasty. Recovery details come from the surgeon.

Documented risks include uneven eyelids, dry eyes if the eye no longer closes fully, bleeding, infection and, rarely, loss of eyelid movement. One study of previously treated ptosis patients found about half needed repeat surgery within 8 to 10 years.

chain: Upper lid raised and crease formed
angle.text: Raising the lid margin shows more of the eye, and the crease defines the lid, making eyes look wider and brighter.

lead: Ptosis is a drooping upper eyelid caused by weakness of the levator muscle or its nerves; it is most often acquired through aponeurosis loosening, and can also be congenital.[1] Double-eyelid surgery creates an upper eyelid crease and is reported as the most common aesthetic procedure in Taiwan and South Korea.[2]

Combining the two operations aims at larger, more open eyes with a defined crease. Surgeons choose the technique by levator function: levator resection or advancement for moderate function, frontalis or Whitnall slings when weak.[1]
Eyelid surgery is generally safe but sits close to the eye.[2]

paras: Levator resection or advancement shortens or reattaches the muscle, generally for limited function around 5 mm or less per Wikipedia; frontalis slings use silicone, nylon or polypropylene to link the lid to the forehead, and Whitnall slings are often chosen for cosmetic results.[1] Surgery is considered when ptosis affects vision or appearance.[1]

It removes fat and linear tissue and may reinforce muscle; epicanthoplasty is often added.[2] Asian eyelids have more fat according to a Korean study cited there.[2] Tape and glue offer a non-surgical alternative.[2] Social pressure around the procedure is discussed in the literature.[2]

Risks are uneven eyelids, dry eyes, bleeding, infection and rarely loss of lid movement; about half of treated patients in one study needed another operation within 8 to 10 years.[1] Successful treatment can improve vision and appearance.[1]
No studies have examined this combined procedure specifically.
